title: Deterministic Verification and a Single-Repair Guardrail for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: a Paired, Shared‑Candidate Study
abstract: We conducted a preregistered, paired experiment to measure how much deterministic verification plus one automated repair (a guarded pipeline) changes the verifier-confirmed correctness of LLM-produced network-configuration candidates compared with the same raw candidates accepted as-is. Using a shared-initial-candidate design and N=250 intent pairs, we generated a single LLM candidate per intent (gpt-5-mini) and then applied a deterministic network validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) with one permitted automated repair. Primary confirmatory analysis (exact McNemar two-sided) shows baseline verifier-pass rate 249/250 (99.6%) and guarded verifier-pass rate 250/250 (100.0%); paired difference = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2%], p=1.0). Only one paired case was discordant and resolved by the single allowed repair. The preregistered primary hypothesis (expecting ≥15 percentage‑point paired deficit) is not supported. We describe the sealed preregistration, deterministic execution contract, analysis, representative artifacts, and limitations. The result indicates that for the synthetic, workflow-constrained tasks studied, a single-shot modern LLM produced nearly universally verifier-acceptable candidates and the guarded pipeline provided negligible incremental paired improvement; we discuss external‑validity limits and propose next steps to probe vendor heterogeneity, larger fault classes, and adaptive-adversary robustness.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are being explored for intent-driven network configuration generation, but their stochastic token sampling raises concerns for operational correctness. Prior work has proposed interposing deterministic verifiers and closed-loop repair between stochastic generation and acceptance (generate–verify–repair, GVR) to reduce mechanically checkable errors [1,2,3]. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment that measures, under shared_initial_candidate semantics, how often deterministic validation plus a single automated repair (the guarded pipeline) converts an existing LLM candidate that would fail verifier checks into a verifier‑pass relative to accepting the same initial candidate without repair. The study was designed to (i) follow a frozen preregistration, (ii) employ modern deterministic network validation, and (iii) preserve the precise shared-candidate comparison required under the track’s semantics. Our contributions: (1) a preregistered, paired evaluation using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator over N=250 intent pairs with machine-verifiable scoring; (2) a full execution and analysis artefact set (shared-generation semantics, validator traces, repair traces, and exact statistical inference); and (3) a documented negative/near-null primary result together with a focused discussion of threats to validity and future experimental directions.
sections.related_work: LLMs for intent→configuration and NetOps automation have been explored in benchmarks and prototypes that show LLMs can create usable draft configurations but often require verification or human oversight [4,5,6]. Architectures that interpose deterministic checkers and repair loops have been proposed for code and configuration domains to reconcile stochastic generation with zero-defect goals [2,7]. Mature deterministic network analyzers and verifiers (e.g., Batfish, header-space and model-checking approaches) are commonly used as validators in research and practice [3,8]. Security work highlights prompt-injection and indirect-injection vectors against LLM-integrated applications and evaluates mitigations that rely on filtering and verifier layers [9]. Our study builds directly on these threads by executing a sealed, paired comparison of raw candidate validity versus final guarded-pipeline validity under shared_initial_candidate semantics.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: The study was preregistered (study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1) and frozen before execution. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics we compared baseline = initial candidate accepted (no repair) versus guarded = same initial candidate after deterministic validation and at most one automated repair call permitted by the execution contract. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Experimental design: deterministic task generator produced N_pairs=250 intent tasks (intent→expected configuration constraints). For each intent the system produced one shared initial generation (gpt-5-mini) which was copied into the baseline episode and into the guarded episode. The guarded path executed the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and, if the validator signalled a mechanistic failure, invoked at most one automated repair attempt using a registered repair template. All prompts, model outputs, validator traces, and repair traces were recorded immutably. Model and tools: declared model gpt-5-mini (provider: openai_responses); deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5; deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution limits: 1 initial generation per task, ≤1 repair per episode; maximum_model_calls=500; actual model calls used=251 (250 initial + 1 repair). Scoring and primary test: the validator produced a boolean verifier_pass per episode. Confirmatory test was exact McNemar two-sided on the paired 2×2 contingency table; 95% CI for paired difference computed by preregistered paired bootstrap percentile (10k resamples, seed preserved). Exclusions and contamination: preregistered deterministic exclusion rules removed parser-blocking syntactic outputs and denylist/private-data cases; no episodes were excluded in execution. All artefacts, manifests, and hashes were archived.
sections.results: Execution and primary outcome: completed_pairs = 250; baseline_success_count = 249 (99.6%); guarded_success_count = 250 (100.0%). Contingency table: n11=249, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0 (notation: n_rc where r=guarded, c=baseline). Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.4 percentage points; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. 95% CI (paired-bootstrap-percentile, 10k resamples) = [0.0, 0.012] (i.e., 0–1.2 percentage points). Only one discordant pair existed and the single allowed repair converted that baseline-failure into a guarded-pass. Secondary planned outputs (violation-type tables, repair-conversion rates) are available in the archived artefacts; overall repair-conversion count = 1/250. No preregistration exclusions or contamination flags triggered; missingness = 0. All reported numerical values match the archived analysis artifacts and deterministic reconciliation manifest.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: The preregistered primary hypothesis (expecting a substantial paired deficit on guarded episodes vs baseline under the sim-to-real framing) is not supported. In these synthetic, workflow-constrained tasks the LLM produced near-universal initial candidates that satisfied the validator; a single automated repair converted the sole verifier-failing initial candidate. This near-null result has three plausible readings (not mutually exclusive): (A) modern LLMs can produce mechanically valid configuration fragments for carefully constrained intents and synthetic topologies; (B) the validator and task generator used here modeled a set of mechanically checkable properties for which LLMs are already highly competent; (C) the experiment’s scope (synthetic tasks, constrained allowed fields, and the specific validator encoding) limited observable failure mass. Threats to validity: Internal — results depend on the chosen prompt template, model version (gpt-5-mini), and single-repair policy; the shared_initial_candidate semantics were followed strictly, so the paired contrast measures validator+repair effect only. Construct — the verifier measured mechanically checkable properties (syntax, prescribed workflow sequences) and may not capture broader semantic correctness or emergent operational risks. External — tasks were deterministic and synthetic; vendor heterogeneity, real production topologies, adversarial retrievals, and adaptive attackers were not exercised. Conclusion validity — the study used a preregistered N=250 paired design with exact paired testing; the observed narrow CI and single discordant case limit claims to the studied task family. Operational implication: For similar constrained intents and verifier scopes, a guarded pipeline with deterministic validation may offer limited paired improvement because modern LLMs can already produce largely verifier-consistent candidates; however, this should not be generalized to broader or adversarial settings without further evidence. Future work: extend to heterogeneous vendor CLIs, larger and noisier topologies, richer validator properties (protocol dynamics), adversarial prompt-injection scenarios, and repeated-repair loops.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure the verifier-detected benefit of deterministic validation plus one automated repair on LLM-generated network-configuration candidates. For the synthetic, workflow-limited tasks studied, initial gpt-5-mini candidates were largely verifier-acceptable (249/250), and the guarded pipeline converted a single failing candidate; the paired improvement was 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2%], p=1.0). The preregistered, artifact-backed null/near-null result implies that GVR-style guardrails may provide small marginal verifier gains in some constrained NetOps task regimes, but broader claims require experiments that exercise vendor heterogeneity, richer failure classes, and adaptive adversaries. All code, raw outputs, verifier traces, and analysis artefacts described in the paper are archived and hashed in the execution bundle for reproducibility and audit.

The research director provided the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and pre-lock infrastructure development; no human edited or rewrote technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock. The autonomous pipeline performed literature verification, preregistration freeze, prompt preservation, model calls, deterministic validation, permitted repair execution, and automated analysis. Pre-lock development artifacts were used only for infrastructure setup and were not treated as empirical evidence; all empirical claims here are supported by post-lock archived execution artifacts and analysis outputs. limitations: Task scope: tasks were synthetically generated and constrained (allowed fields/workflow policies). Results do not directly generalize to large, heterogeneous production topologies or broad, unconstrained intents.

Validator coverage: the deterministic validator measured mechanically checkable properties (syntax, prescribed workflow sequences). Semantic correctness beyond encoded constraints (e.g., performance, emergent protocol dynamics) was not assessed.
Model and tooling scope: a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation were used; multi-model or alternate-validator generality is untested.
Adversary and prompt-injection effects: adaptive prompt-injection and retrieval-based attacks were not evaluated in this confirmatory run and remain an open threat vector.
Single-repair policy: only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi-iteration repair loops or human-in-the-loop escalation were not exercised and may yield different outcomes.
